strings.name: Hakainde Hichilema
strings.role: President of Zambia and leader of the United Party for National Development
strings.summary: Hakainde Hichilema is a Zambian businessman, farmer and politician who began leading the United Party for National Development in 2006 and won the presidency on his sixth attempt in 2021. His government has pursued school-fee reform and debt restructuring. He began a second term in 2026 amid controversy over electoral procedures, opposition detention and civil rights.
strings.coverageNote: Information checked through 18 November 2026. His current office is confirmed by the second-term inauguration on 1 September 2026 and subsequent government documents. Amnesty International continued to raise concerns over opposition detention on 17 November; official election results, observers’ assessments and human-rights allegations are recorded separately.
strings.influence.rationale: Elected to Zambia’s presidency, he has participated in debt restructuring, mining and economic-recovery policies, influencing discussions of African development.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born on 4 June 1962 in the Monze district of southern Zambia, he earned a bachelor’s degree in economics and business administration at the University of Zambia in 1986 and later an MBA in finance and business strategy at the University of Birmingham in the United Kingdom. No unverified MBA graduation year is supplied.
strings.facts.f2.label: Business background
strings.facts.f2.value: He worked in accounting and business-consultancy management, operated ranches and invested in tourism and other sectors. His leadership posts at Coopers & Lybrand and Grant Thornton concerned their Zambian operations, not the global leadership of either network.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Debt treatment and economic recovery
strings.highlights.h1.text: His governing agenda includes restoring fiscal and debt sustainability, attracting investment and improving public services. Completion of the Eurobond exchange in 2024 was a concrete step, while treatment of other creditors was still progressing and severe drought was affecting agriculture and electricity generation.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Democratic pledges and civil-rights controversy
strings.highlights.h2.text: At his 2021 inauguration he pledged to uphold the rule of law and fundamental freedoms. Opposition detentions and barriers to legal redress after the 2026 election drew criticism. On 17 November Amnesty International called for the release of 18 opposition figures and raised allegations of arbitrary detention and mistreatment.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Beginning a second presidential term
strings.timeline.t1.text: He took the oath at the National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka. Voting had taken place on 13 August and the electoral commission declared him the winner on 18 August. AP and Reuters also reported opposition challenges to the results, detentions and obstacles to legal appeals.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Settlement of the Eurobond exchange
strings.timeline.t2.text: The IMF confirmed that Zambia settled the bond exchange on 11 June, after reaching an agreement in principle in March and launching consent solicitation in May. This was a step in sovereign-debt restructuring, not cancellation of all debt or completion of every creditor agreement.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Implementing expanded free education
strings.timeline.t3.text: The government removed relevant school fees at pre-primary, primary and secondary levels and increased school grants. The reform expanded earlier free-education arrangements. A 2025 Parliamentary Budget Office brief still identified overcrowding, teacher-deployment issues and shortcomings in education-data quality.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Becoming Zambia’s seventh president
strings.timeline.t4.text: He was sworn in after defeating Edgar Lungu in the 12 August election, following five unsuccessful presidential campaigns. His inaugural address set out goals for economic recovery, employment and the rule of law; campaign commitments and subsequent implementation require separate assessment.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Released after treason proceedings were discontinued
strings.timeline.t5.text: He had been detained in April over a motorcade incident and charged with treason, and was released in August after prosecutors terminated the proceedings. Discontinuing a prosecution differs from an acquittal on the merits and was not completion of a prison sentence for treason.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Taking over leadership of the UPND
strings.timeline.t6.text: After party founder Anderson Mazoka died, he was selected as leader and presidential candidate, beginning a long career in opposition politics. Taking over an existing party did not make him its founder.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Leading Grant Thornton’s Zambian operations
strings.timeline.t7.text: He entered the top management role at Grant Thornton Zambia and served until 2006. His consultancy-management experience preceded formal party leadership; the international brand name does not make the role a global chief-executive position.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Heading Coopers & Lybrand’s Zambian operations
strings.timeline.t8.text: He rose to local chief executive in the accounting and business-consultancy industry, serving until 1998. Institutional biographies identify this experience as important background to his move from business management into public politics.
